lead: Overnight lip and eye masks are leave-on products, usually a thick balm, gel, cream or patch, applied before bed and left on while sleeping. People use them to wake up with softer, smoother-looking lips and more hydrated skin under the eyes, so that dryness, flaking and fine dehydration lines look less obvious in the morning.

They work on general moisturiser principles. Occlusives such as petrolatum form a film that slows water loss, and humectants draw water into the skin.[1] Lip balm formulations rely mainly on an occlusive layer that seals in moisture and shields the lips from dry air, cold and wind; lip skin is thin and often shows dryness first.[2] The skin of the lower eyelid is also very thin, which is one reason underlying vessels and dryness show there.[3]

The overnight format gives the product several hours of contact without being rubbed off by eating, drinking or talking. Sleep masks that cover the eyes to block light are a separate item.[4] No clinical trial of the branded overnight lip or eye masks was located.

chain: Thick occlusive or hydrating layer applied before bed
Reduced water loss from lips and eyelid skin overnight
Softer lips and plumper-looking under-eye skin by morning
angle.text: The mask holds moisture against lips and eye-area skin for hours, which makes lips look smoother and the under-eye area look less dry and crinkled when the product is removed in the morning. The effect is on hydration and surface texture.

infobox: Lip sleeping mask, cream eye mask, hydrogel eye patch

paras: Products range from petrolatum- or wax-based lip balms to gel or hydrogel under-eye patches and creamy eye masks. Ointments are more occlusive than creams, which are more occlusive than lotions.[1]

Lip balms are commonly built from waxes such as beeswax, carnauba or candelilla plus lanolin, paraffin or petrolatum, and some add flavouring, fragrance or sunscreen.[2] Eye products often add humectants and sometimes caffeine or vitamin C, which Wikipedia lists among ingredients used for the under-eye area.[3]

Occlusives cut transepidermal water loss; a petrolatum layer can reduce it by roughly half to three-quarters for several hours.[1] Petroleum jelly is described on Wikipedia as a barrier that slows water loss and helps prevent chapped lips, and the American Academy of Dermatology is cited as recommending it for keeping injured skin moist.[5] Humectants draw in water but can leave deeper layers drier unless paired with an occlusive.[1]

Dark circles under the eyes have several causes, including thin skin, pigmentation, allergies, sleep loss and ageing, and a moisturising mask addresses surface dryness rather than those underlying factors.[3]

Lip balm is traced to ancient Egyptian beeswax-based salves; physician Charles Browne Fleet is credited with the 1880s product named ChapStick, followed by Carmex in 1937, a flavoured balm from Bonne Bell in 1973 and Burt's Bees in 1991.[2] Petroleum jelly was patented by Robert Chesebrough in 1872 and sold as Vaseline.[5] The overnight lip-mask format, popular in Korean and wider skincare marketing, is a more recent presentation of the same occlusive principle.

Moisturisers can cause contact dermatitis from fragrances or other ingredients, and 'hypoallergenic' is not a regulated term.[1] Paraffin-based products are a fire hazard near open flames.[1] In 2015 the German consumer group Stiftung Warentest reported mineral oil aromatic hydrocarbons in some lip products, including Vaseline, and advised against mineral-oil-based lip care, a finding reported on Wikipedia.[2][5] Some physicians have suggested lip balms may be habit-forming or drying, a claim Wikipedia says professionals dispute.[2]
No studies found on overnight lip or eye masks. Research on general occlusive moisturisers is summarised under how it works.[1]

name: Overnight lip/eye masks

card.summary: Thick balms and gels left on overnight for lips and eyes; plain moisturiser logic, no trials of the masks themselves.
card.aka: Lip sleeping mask, eye sleeping mask

quick.overview:
These are rich moisturising products worn overnight on the lips or around the eyes. People use them to wake up with less dryness.

The general principle of occlusive moisturisers is documented, but no studies of the branded masks were found.
quick.mechanism: Occlusive ingredients trap moisture by slowing water loss, while humectants attract water. Effects are on hydration, not structure.
quick.risks: Irritation or allergic contact dermatitis from fragrance or other ingredients is possible. Paraffin-based products are flammable.
